analysis|02-12|1554|Αποκεφαλίζεται η Λαίδη Τζέιν Γκρέι|Lady Jane Grey is beheaded|In the mid-16th century the English succession was unstable, since King Edward VI was a minor and the throne could pass to people connected with the Tudor family. Jane Grey, granddaughter of the sister of Henry VIII, had been put forward by her supporters as heir, in an attempt to prevent the return of the Catholic Mary to the throne. This policy was dangerous and unstable. // Jane reigned for only a few days in 1553, as the "nine days' queen", before Mary I came to the throne. The new queen quickly gained the support of the people, and Jane was arrested and held in the Tower of London. On 12 February 1554 she was executed in the Tower, at only seventeen years of age, after a trial on a charge of treason. // Jane's fate is regarded as a symbol of the tragic dependence of young people on the political factions of the era. Her execution shows how harsh the successive crises of the English monarchy could be. Today her story occupies many scholars, who examine her role within a particularly complex political setting. The story begins with the conflicts of the courts and ends with the tragic personal fate of a young woman.

analysis|02-12|1809|Γεννιούνται ο Λίνκολν και ο Δαρβίνος|Lincoln and Darwin are born|In the early 19th century Europe and America were in a period of great change, with science and politics developing at the same time. Slavery in the United States was one of the central issues of the era, while the natural sciences were beginning to shape the basic ideas about the evolution of species. The two people who were born on the same day were to deeply influence these developments. // On 12 February 1809 Abraham Lincoln was born in Kentucky in the United States, and Charles Darwin in Britain. Lincoln grew up in a poor farming family and later became president, and his policy led to the abolition of slavery. Darwin, the son of a doctor, studied natural history and travelled to many parts of the world, recording observations about species. // Lincoln was a central figure of the American Civil War and of the abolition of slavery, while Darwin formulated the theory of natural selection, which changed scientific thought. The coincidence of their birth day has often become a subject of historical reference, because it shows how two different paths contributed to shaping the modern world. Comparing the two paths helps to show how politics and science influenced the same era.

analysis|02-12|1817|Η νίκη στο Τσακαμπούκο|The victory at Chacabuco|At the beginning of the 19th century Chile and Argentina were under Spanish rule, but the independence movements had intensified after 1810. José de San Martín, an officer with experience in the European wars, organised an army in Argentina and planned to cross the Andes to help the Chilean revolutionaries. The crossing of the mountains was an enormous challenge, with heavy losses in the army. // On 12 February 1817 the patriot army defeated the Spanish soldiers at the battle of Chacabuco, near Santiago. The victory opened the way to the capital and strengthened the morale of the revolutionaries. The battle is regarded as one of the decisive events of the Chilean struggle for independence. // This victory led to a new phase of the struggle, with Chile gaining independence shortly afterwards, and the cooperation of the two countries became a symbol of the continental revolution. San Martín is today one of the central figures of Latin American history. The battle recalls the importance of strategic boldness in critical moments. The analysis of the campaign shows how important the organisation and command of the troops were. The victory strengthened the morale of the revolutionaries and influenced the diplomacy of the region.

analysis|02-12|1909|Ιδρύεται η NAACP|The NAACP is founded|At the beginning of the 20th century African Americans in the United States faced racial segregation, violence and exclusion from many rights, particularly in the southern states. The legal barriers were severe, and the need for organised action became ever more pressing. After great uprisings and racial clashes, many citizens sought new ways to defend their rights. // On 12 February 1909 the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People, known as the NAACP, was founded. The organisation brought together white and Black supporters and aimed at legal justice and political equality. Through its legal strategy the NAACP became one of the most important bodies of the era. // The NAACP fought major court battles, among them cases that strengthened civil rights. Its activity played a role in shaping the civil rights movement of the 1960s. Today the organisation is regarded as a historic pillar of anti-racist action in the United States. The anti-racist activity of the organisation is a point of reference for researchers of political history. The organisation was later linked with significant court victories concerning education and the vote, and it remained a point of reference for the generations of activists that followed.

analysis|02-12|1912|Παραιτείται ο τελευταίος αυτοκράτορας|The last emperor abdicates|At the beginning of the 20th century China was in deep crisis, with the Qing dynasty weakened after defeats and uprisings. The revolutionary movement, led by Sun Yat-sen, demanded democracy and national independence. The reforms of the court were far too slow, and society wanted radical change. // In February 1912 Puyi, who was only six years old, abdicated the throne, and the Qing dynasty came to an end. The abdication was accompanied by an agreement that kept certain privileges for the court. The decision opened the way to the democratic creation of a new political system. // The abdication marked the end of imperial China, which had been governed by emperors for centuries. The country passed into a period of political instability and civil conflicts, before the establishment of the People's Republic. The event is regarded as the beginning of modern Chinese history. This abdication is one of the important milestones of China's political history in the 20th century. The fall of the monarchy left behind a power vacuum and a long period of instability that affected the economy and society. The reform efforts that followed were debated for decades. This period left deep traces on the political culture of the country and on its relationship with institutional reform.

analysis|02-12|1947|Το «New Look» του Κριστιάν Ντιόρ|Christian Dior's "New Look"|After the Second World War European fashion was in a period of restriction, with austere lines and short dresses, because of the shortage of fabrics and economic difficulties. Paris had lost part of its position as a centre of fashion during the war. Women wished to return to more refined and feminine clothing. // In February 1947 Christian Dior presented his first collection, under the name "New Look". The clothes had full skirts, a narrow waist and emphasised shoulders, and represented a bold return to richness of shapes. The collection provoked intense debate, between admiration and criticism for its consumption of fabric. // The collection put Paris back at the top of international fashion and set the course of fashion for the years that followed. The House of Dior developed into a global brand, and the "New Look" is regarded as a landmark of postwar fashion. Its influence extends to this day in the collections of many designers. The collection is still discussed as an example of the relationship between fashion and economic conditions. The events of the period showed that fashion could work also as a cultural and economic instrument for the whole country.

analysis|02-12|1950|Ιδρύεται η Ευρωπαϊκή Ένωση Ραδιοτηλεόρασης|The European Broadcasting Union is founded|After the Second World War European public radio and television networks needed cooperation to exchange programmes, technical know-how and information. Broadcasting technology was developing quickly, and the organisations were asking for common standards. Public bodies wished to keep their independence from the commercial market. // On 12 February 1950 the organisation that became known as the EBU was founded, with the aim of uniting the public radio and television bodies of Europe. The organisation undertook to coordinate technical matters and joint productions. This cooperation facilitated the exchange of broadcasts and gave a boost to European television. // The EBU has since organised the Eurovision Song Contest, which became one of the best-known television events in Europe. The organisation continues to promote cooperation among public media, the quality of programmes and common technical standards. Its history shows the importance of cooperation in the European integration of culture. The cooperation of public bodies was a basic element of European television history. This cooperation continued with new structures, which strengthened the spread of cultural programmes throughout Europe. This cooperation was an example for the shaping of common European policies in the fields of information and education.

analysis|02-13|1542|Εκτελείται η Αικατερίνη Χάουαρντ|Catherine Howard is executed|In the early 16th century the English court was full of rivalries, and King Henry VIII had already married four times, with the aim of securing an heir. Catherine Howard, young and from a great aristocratic family, married the king in 1540, while the political balance of the court was fragile. Her enemies had strong influence in the palace. // Catherine was accused of adultery and of earlier relationships before the marriage, and these charges led to a trial that was harsh for her and for her family. On 13 February 1542 she was beheaded in the Tower of London, in accordance with the royal decision. The execution took place without much public discussion at the palace. // Catherine's fate is regarded as characteristic of the harshness of the English court of the era and of the dependence of wives on the politics of royal power. Her story is often presented as an example of the vulnerability of women within the context of succession. Today her figure is examined by historians who study the Tudor court. Her story is linked with the political balances of a court where every marriage had a political dimension. The scientific development of the era was closely linked with the social and political conditions of the time.

analysis|02-13|1633|Ο Γαλιλαίος φτάνει στη Ρώμη για τη δίκη του|Galileo arrives in Rome for his trial|In the early 17th century the science of astronomy was challenging the old views about the universe, and the theory of Copernicus, which placed the Sun at the centre, was becoming ever more widespread. The Catholic Church regarded these views as contrary to the Scriptures, and the clash between scientific research and theological orthodoxy was intense. Galileo had already discussed his ideas publicly. // In 1632 Galileo published his work "Dialogue", which compares the two systems, and the Inquisition summoned him to Rome. On 13 February 1633 he arrived in the city, to be tried for his views on the motion of the Earth around the Sun. The trial followed over the next few weeks under a strict procedure. // The trial ended with his condemnation to house arrest and with the demand that he renounce his views. The case of Galileo became a symbol of the clash between science and the authority of the Church. The Catholic Church later acknowledged its errors in its handling of the case. The case is still discussed as a lesson on the relationship between faith and science. This crisis showed how critical the diplomatic balances of the era were for the historical development of peoples.

analysis|02-13|1945|Ο βομβαρδισμός της Δρέσδης|The bombing of Dresden|In the last years of the Second World War Germany was in full retreat, but the Allies continued their strategic attacks on cities and industrial centres. Dresden was an important city, with cultural heritage and railway junctions, which were used for the movement of troops and supplies. The military reasons were debated intensely later. // On 13 February 1945 British and American aircraft attacked the city, with bombing raids that continued for several days. The attack caused large fires, which destroyed a large part of the city and its monuments. Human losses were very heavy, with tens of thousands dead. // The bombing of Dresden remains in history as one of the most controversial events of the war, with debates about strategic necessity and the morality of the outcome. The city was later rebuilt, and its destruction has become a symbol of the suffering of war for the Germans and for European memory. The destruction of the city remains a subject of research for historians of the era. This decision was an example of the relationship between power and religion. Historians still discuss the motives of the leaders of the time. This episode is today taught as an example of the relationship between power, institutions and public opinion of the era.

analysis|02-13|1960|Η Γαλλία δοκιμάζει την πρώτη της ατομική βόμβα|France tests its first atomic bomb|After the Second World War France sought to acquire its own nuclear capability, in order to maintain its prestige and independence in the new world of the Cold War. The development of the nuclear programme was a political priority, and the country invested in research centres. Algeria was then a French colony, and the Sahara desert was chosen for the tests. // On 13 February 1960 the first test took place, named "Gerboise Bleue", in an area of the Sahara. The test made France the fourth nuclear power in the world, after the United States, the Soviet Union and Britain. This success strengthened the national prestige of the country. // The test contributed to the shaping of the French deterrence strategy, which remained a basic element of its foreign policy. However, the nuclear tests caused reactions and contamination of the area, and the issue continues to develop to this day. Algeria gained its independence a few years later, in 1962. The test remains a point of reference for the relationship of France with its colonial past. This battle and the reaction of the era strengthened the importance of national independence for the peoples of the region. This battle is still discussed for its place in the wider course of the war and for its significance for France.

analysis|02-13|1984|Ο Τσερνιένκο ηγέτης της ΕΣΣΔ|Chernenko becomes leader of the USSR|In the early 1980s the Soviet Union was experiencing economic stagnation and leadership instability, as the leaders of the era grew old and died within a short period. The leadership of the Communist Party faced many challenges, and the search for a new direction was intense. Succession was often opaque and depended on internal balances. // Konstantin Chernenko was elected general secretary of the Communist Party on 13 February 1984, after the death of Yuri Andropov. His election took place at a time when the government had already grown old, and it was regarded as a transitional solution. The new leadership faced serious problems in the economy and in foreign affairs. // Chernenko's term was short, since he died in 1985, and the country chose Gorbachev shortly afterwards, who began reforms with glasnost and perestroika. This period shows the deep crisis of the Soviet system before the reforms of the late 1980s. This succession marked the end of an era in Soviet politics. The scientific community of the time reacted to his ideas with growing interest, and his work is discussed to this day. This clash showed the tension between scientific truth and the institutional balances of the era.

analysis|02-13|2001|Φονικός σεισμός στο Ελ Σαλβαδόρ|Deadly earthquake in El Salvador|El Salvador is a small country of Central America, located in an area of intense seismic activity because of the convergence of tectonic plates. Earthquakes are a frequent phenomenon, and many houses are built with materials that cannot withstand strong tremors. The society had already experienced disasters in the past. // On 13 February 2001 a powerful earthquake struck the region, with its epicentre in the Pacific, and caused widespread destruction to houses, roads and infrastructure. The earthquake killed hundreds of people, while many were left homeless. International rescue and aid teams hurried to assist the local authorities. // This disaster highlighted the need for better earthquake protection and for emergency plans. Reconstruction followed with the support of international organisations and of civil society. The earthquake is remembered as one of the most serious natural disasters in the country in the early 21st century. This story shows the importance of preparation for natural disasters. This practice was part of a wider change in communications and in the administration of the era. Historians regard it as an example of the progress of societies. The situation described affected the lives of citizens and the way in which the city's services were organised.

analysis|02-14|1779|Σκοτώνεται ο Τζέιμς Κουκ|James Cook is killed|At the end of the 18th century James Cook was already known as a naval explorer, who had charted important areas of the Pacific Ocean for the British Empire. His voyages included contacts with the peoples of the islands, which were often complex and full of misunderstandings. Relations with the indigenous inhabitants were sometimes strained. // During his stay in Hawaii, Cook came into conflict with locals in Kealakekua Bay, on 14 February 1779. The dispute developed into a clash, during which Cook himself was killed, together with several sailors of the crew. The news shocked the British and the naval circles. // Cook's death became a subject of discussion about the relations between explorers and indigenous peoples, and his figure remains controversial. Today Hawaii remembers the event and its relationship with European exploration, which profoundly changed the history of the region. The exploration of the area left long-lasting traces on the relationship of the islands with Europe. The discussions around this process have returned many times, and its experience is used today as a lesson about institutions. The clarity of rules remains a basic objective of democratic states.

analysis|02-14|1876|Ο Γκράχαμ Μπελ καταθέτει αίτηση για το τηλέφωνο|Graham Bell files a patent application for the telephone|In the mid-19th century telegraphy was the basic means of rapid communication over long distances, while many inventors were trying to transmit the human voice by electrical signals. The idea was particularly attractive for businesses and governments, and inventors competed for the patent. This competitive race was intense in the United States. // On 14 February 1876 Alexander Graham Bell filed a patent application for the voice transmission device, which is regarded as the first telephone. A few hours later Elisha Gray filed an application for a similar device, and the dispute over priority became widely known. This case became the subject of many discussions and legal disputes. // Bell eventually won the patent right, and his invention became the basis for the development of telephone networks. The spread of the telephone changed communication in cities and in the countryside, and affected people's way of life. The history of the telephone also brings to the fore the importance of priority in invention. The spread of the telephone marked a new era in communications. The history of this recall is linked with the progress of the sciences and with the development of wider political disputes. This invention paved the way for new forms of communication, which in time shaped everyday life.

analysis|02-14|1912|Η Αριζόνα γίνεται πολιτεία|Arizona becomes a state|At the beginning of the 20th century Arizona was still a territory of the United States, with a growing population, mining and agriculture. The admission of the area as a state was a subject of debate for years, while residents demanded full political rights. Congress considered the question repeatedly, with differing views on the form of government of the territory. // On 14 February 1912 Arizona officially became the 48th state of the United States, with its own constitution and its own state institutions. The admission completed the progress of the western territories that had remained outside the union of states. The new state took part in the political life of the country immediately. // Arizona's admission closed the period of territorial areas in the western part of the United States, and the 48th state became a model for the development of the region. Economic activity and population grew steadily in the following decades. This date is regarded as a turning point in the history of the United States. This admission left behind a modern state system with its own institutions. The era showed how slowly the laws on equality of citizens changed, and this debate continued for decades. These changes came gradually, and society adapted slowly to the new legal balances.

analysis|02-14|1929|Η Σφαγή του Αγίου Βαλεντίνου|The Saint Valentine's Day Massacre|In the late 1920s Chicago was one of the centres of organised crime, with gangs competing for control of illegal alcohol during the Prohibition period. Al Capone was the best-known leader of the era, and rivalries with other gangs were violent and frequent. The situation had become a political issue. // On 14 February 1929 men connected with Capone killed seven members of a rival gang in a garage in the city. The event shocked public opinion and showed how violent the gang had become. The massacre became a matter of great publicity. // The massacre contributed to a change in public policy against organised crime, and the police and federal authorities were strengthened. Capone was eventually convicted of tax evasion, but not for the massacre. The event became a central element in the history of American crime of the era. The affair remained in popular culture as a symbol of the Prohibition era. The development of this case became a subject of study on the relationship between violence and the political life of American cities. This case gave rise to discussions about the regulation of weapons and the safety of cities.

analysis|02-14|1952|Ξεκινούν οι Χειμερινοί Ολυμπιακοί Αγώνες του Όσλο|The Oslo Winter Olympics open|After the Second World War the Olympic world was trying to return to normality, and the Winter Games sought new momentum after the years of conflict. Norway, with its long tradition in skiing and winter sport, emerged as a natural choice for hosting. The preparation of the facilities and transport required considerable effort. // On 14 February 1952 the sixth Winter Olympic Games opened in Oslo, with the participation of hundreds of athletes from about thirty countries. The events included skiing, skating and other winter challenges, which attracted large crowds. The ceremony and the organisation were regarded as successful. // The Oslo Games contributed to the development of winter sport and to the strengthening of the Olympic movement after the war. The organisation showed that the Winter Games could develop into a great international festival. Norway remains in history as a country with a strong tradition in winter sports. The organisation of these Games set an example for later winter events in Europe. The history of these Games is linked with the way major events shape the image of a country abroad. The organisation of these Games required particular effort from the local authorities and from the athletes themselves.

analysis|02-14|1989|Το φετβά του Χομεϊνί κατά του Σαλμάν Ρούσντι|Khomeini's fatwa against Salman Rushdie|In 1988 the British-Indian writer Salman Rushdie published the novel "The Satanic Verses", which many Muslims regarded as offensive to Islam. The book provoked demonstrations and protests in various countries, while freedom of expression became a subject of international debate. The Iranian leadership reacted strongly to the work. // On 14 February 1989 the supreme leader of Iran, Khomeini, issued a fatwa calling on Muslims to kill the author and the publishers of the work. The decision provoked worldwide reaction and shock in literary and political circles. Rushdie was forced to live under strict protection for years. // The fatwa became a symbol of the clash between freedom of speech and religious criticism, with consequences for Iran's diplomacy and for its relations with the West. The affair is still discussed in the context of the limits of freedom of expression. Rushdie continued to write and to speak in public, and his work remained a point of reference in literature. The case remains one of the best-known examples of the clash over freedom of expression. The debate over freedom of expression continues in many states, and the case remains a point of reference.

analysis|02-14|1990|Η φωτογραφία «Ωχρή Μπλε Τελεία»|The "Pale Blue Dot" photograph|In 1977 the Voyager spacecraft had been launched, with a mission to explore the outer planets of the solar system and to continue beyond them. The instruments of the craft had been designed to record images and data over a long period. These images were collected for the scientific recording of the solar system. // On 14 February 1990 Voyager 1, at a distance of about six billion kilometres, photographed the Earth as a tiny dot within a sunbeam. The image became known as the "Pale Blue Dot", after the idea of Carl Sagan, who wished to emphasise the place of humanity in the universe. The photograph went beyond the limits of science. // The image became a symbol of the unity of the human species and of the fragility of our planet. Environmental awareness and the idea of shared responsibility were strengthened through this photograph. Today it remains one of the best-known images ever taken by a spacecraft. The image continues to be used as a reminder of the Earth's place in the universe. The mission gave scientists new data about the solar system and the properties of its bodies. This discovery opens the way to new observations and to understanding how celestial bodies evolve.

analysis|02-14|1994|Συμφωνία για την καταστροφή των πυρηνικών όπλων της Ουκρανίας|Agreement on the dismantling of Ukraine's nuclear weapons|After the dissolution of the Soviet Union in 1991, Ukraine found itself with a significant nuclear arsenal on its territory, which had belonged to the former USSR. The country faced concerns about security, the economy and its relations with Russia and the West. The United States and Russia were worried about the risk of the spread of the weapons. // In 1994 the leaders of the United States, Russia and Ukraine signed an agreement that provided for the handover of Ukraine's nuclear weapons to Russia and for the giving of guarantees of the country's security and independence. The agreement combined denuclearisation with economic and political benefits. // The agreement is regarded as an important step for the non-proliferation of nuclear weapons in the world. However, the guarantees that were given later were questioned, since the Russian invasions of 2014 and 2022 raised questions about their reliability. The history of this agreement remains central to the debate on nuclear security. The discussion about the reliability of international guarantees continues to this day. The fate of the people of the region was deeply affected by the consequences of the agreement, and the debate about its aftermath continues. International negotiations on security and arms control were among the central issues of the era.

analysis|02-15|1564|Γεννιέται ο Γαλιλαίος|Galileo is born|In the mid-16th century Italy was divided into many states, while the Renaissance had brought new ideas about art, science and human thought. Pisa was a city with a university and a lively intellectual life. Galileo's family was educated and was involved with music. // Galileo was born in Pisa on 15 February 1564, the son of a musician with intellectual interests. He studied medicine at the university of the city, but he was more interested in mathematics and physics. The development of his interests led him to a career that changed science. // Galileo was a pioneer of the experimental method and of observing the sky with the telescope. His discoveries, such as the moons of Jupiter and the phases of Venus, strengthened the ideas of Copernicus. His work is regarded as a milestone in the making of modern science, and his figure is linked with the way we see the universe today. His life was closely bound up with the intellectual conflicts of his time. The event was widely recorded by the sources of the era and is regarded today as an important milestone for the study of science. The life of this great scientist was linked with an era in which knowledge could be challenged or promoted by the authorities.

analysis|02-15|1835|Η Σερβία παίρνει το πρώτο της Σύνταγμα|Serbia adopts its first constitution|In the early 19th century Serbia was part of the Ottoman Empire, but the uprisings of 1804 and 1815 had led to autonomy and to a first form of state organisation. The leadership of Miloš Obrenović strengthened the control of the country, while the need for a defined legal order was intense. Society demanded stability and institutions. // On 15 February 1835 the Serbian Assembly adopted the first constitution of the country, known as the Constitution of the Presentation, after the name of the related feast. The text defined the position of the ruler and the organs of administration, although it was limited by Ottoman and Russian influences. The adoption of the constitution was an important step in national organisation. // The constitution remained in force for a short time, since it met with reactions and was revised later. However, it became a symbol of Serbia's national revival and a point of reference for later constitutional struggles. Its history shows the complex path of the country towards a modern state. The adoption was linked with the need for legal stability after years of war. This text is still studied as an example of the first attempts at constitutional organisation in the Balkans. The debate over the form of government and the rights of citizens was intense during the period, and the text reflects those views.

analysis|02-15|1898|Εκρήγνυται το θωρηκτό Maine|The battleship Maine explodes|At the end of the 19th century Cuba was a Spanish colony, and the uprising for independence had escalated. The United States followed developments with interest, and public opinion often supported the rebels through the press of the era. The region had become a field of tension between the two countries. // On 15 February 1898 the American battleship Maine sank after an explosion in the harbour of Havana, with the loss of many crew members. The cause of the explosion remained a subject of debate, and the American press immediately accused the Spanish. The incident provoked great emotion in the United States. // The destruction of the Maine led to the Spanish-American War, which began about two months later and ended with the defeat of Spain. The event strengthened the position of the United States as a world power, and Cuba remained under American occupation until 1902. This affair remains one of the best-known episodes of American history. This story is also discussed as an example of how news reporting can influence politics. This disaster changed political debates about the safety of ships and the responsibility of states. The crisis that followed led to new rules and to international discussions about the safety of ships and harbours.

analysis|02-15|1942|Πέφτει η Σιγκαπούρη|Singapore falls|At the beginning of the Second World War Singapore was a British fortress in Asia, which was regarded as a strong point of defence for Britain's naval supremacy in the region. Japan had attacked Malaya and was advancing its troops to the south. The defence of Singapore relied on fortifications that had been designed mainly for attack from the sea. // On 15 February 1942 the British garrison surrendered to the Japanese, after a short but intense campaign. The surrender was shocking for Britain, since Singapore had been regarded as impregnable. Thousands of soldiers were taken prisoner, and the city came under Japanese occupation. // The fall of Singapore is regarded as one of the greatest defeats in British history, and it showed the limits of colonial power in Asia. The defeat had deep consequences for British prestige in the region and strengthened independence movements. Singapore was liberated after the war and later became an independent state. This defeat remained in British memory as a symbol of fragile colonial power. The fall of the city affected the way the British understood the security of their empire. The loss of the port and the fortresses was particularly painful, because it affected trade and the strategic balance of Asia.

analysis|02-15|1946|Παρουσιάζεται ο ENIAC|The ENIAC is unveiled|After the Second World War the United States invested in the development of computing machines for military purposes, such as ballistics and data processing. The machines available until then were limited, slow and difficult to use. The need for faster calculations was intense in the research centres. // On 15 February 1946 the ENIAC was unveiled at the University of Pennsylvania. It was the first general-purpose electronic computer, which could be programmed for various tasks, and it used thousands of electronic valves. The machine occupied a large space and consumed a great deal of power. // The ENIAC paved the way for the development of modern computers, and its architecture influenced the systems that followed. The ability to programme a computer for several tasks became a basic element of computing. The machine is today regarded as a milestone in the history of technology and of the digital age. Its contribution is widely recognised by historians of computing. This invention became the first step towards a new generation of computers, which transformed science and everyday life. The developments that followed gradually made it a basic tool of modern society. The following decades brought new computers of smaller size and greater speed, which changed people's lives.

analysis|02-15|1989|Αποχωρούν οι Σοβιετικοί από το Αφγανιστάν|The Soviets withdraw from Afghanistan|At the end of the 1970s the Soviet Union had intervened in Afghanistan to support the pro-Soviet regime, which was facing internal uprisings. The war was difficult, with guerrillas who had the support of many external powers. Soviet public opinion was increasingly tired of the losses and the cost. // In February 1989 the last Soviet troops left Afghanistan, after about ten years of war. The withdrawal was completed in accordance with the agreements that had been reached, and the event was regarded as a great defeat for Moscow. These developments influenced the course of Soviet politics. // The withdrawal did not bring peace to Afghanistan, since civil conflicts continued for years. The war left deep marks on the country and on Soviet society. This experience is discussed as an example of the limits of military intervention in complex societies. The withdrawal marked the end of a difficult period for the Soviet Union. The retreat affected the lives of the people of Afghanistan, who continued to face violence and insecurity for many years. This experience left in Soviet society a sense of weariness and of questioning of state policy.

analysis|02-15|1989|Η Σοβιετική Ένωση αποσύρει τα στρατεύματά της|The Soviet Union withdraws its troops|The war in Afghanistan was among the most costly conflicts for the Soviet Union, with strong political and military dimensions. The presence of the Red Army had provoked resistance from Afghan guerrillas, who received support from abroad. International public opinion criticised the military intervention, and in Moscow the political leadership was seeking a way out. // The last Soviet soldier crossed the border and left Afghanistan in February 1989, after ten years of war. The withdrawal was in accordance with the Geneva Accords, which had been signed under the mediation of the United Nations. The moment marked the end of a very difficult period. // The withdrawal left behind a state shattered by war, and the civil war continued for several years. For the Soviet Union the war was one of the causes of the internal changes that followed in the next decade. The event is regarded as a turning point in the course of Soviet power.
